explanation.whyCorrect: Although aspirin is normally the first step in treatment of suspected myocardial infarction, the brick lists a history of ASA-related anaphylactic reaction among the contraindications to aspirin. This patient's prior hypotension, angioedema, and wheezing after aspirin represent such a reaction, so aspirin should be withheld.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chewed regular aspirin is the standard ACS approach, but it is contraindicated in a patient with prior ASA anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A lower dose or enteric coating does not remove the anaphylaxis contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamine premedication is not described as a way to overcome the contraindication of prior ASA-related anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A topical salicylate provides no antithrombotic benefit and still exposes a patient with prior salicylate anaphylaxis to the drug.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with asthma, chronic rhinitis, and nasal polyps develops severe respiratory distress after taking aspirin. Which of the following best characterizes the mechanism of this reaction?

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity to acetylsalicylate

explanation.summary: AERD is a non-immunological reaction caused by COX-1 inhibition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease involves respiratory distress and, per the brick, is a non-immunological reaction due to COX-1 inhibition. The resulting increase in pro-inflammatory leukotrienes drives bronchoconstriction, vascular leaks, mucus secretion, and inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement activation is not implicated; the reaction stems from enzyme (COX-1) inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AERD is not an IgE-mediated allergy; it is explicitly described as non-immunological.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune-complex deposition is not the mechanism; no immunological process is involved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A delayed T-cell response does not explain the rapid, COX-1-dependent respiratory reaction.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease develops bronchoconstriction, vascular leakage, and increased mucus secretion after aspirin exposure. The accompanying airway inflammation in this condition is mediated predominantly by which of the following cells?

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD8+ T cells and natural killer cells

explanation.summary: AERD involves increased eosinophilic and mast cell-mediated inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that AERD can cause bronchoconstriction, vascular leaks, mucus secretion, and increased eosinophilic and mast cell-mediated inflammation, driven by the rise in pro-inflammatory leukotrienes after COX-1 inhibition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells and plasma cells (antibody production) are not the effectors; AERD is non-immunological.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Basophils and platelets are not the cell types named in the brick's description of AERD inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytotoxic T cells and NK cells are not implicated in the leukotriene-driven inflammation of AERD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils and macrophages are not the cells the brick associates with AERD inflammation.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man had a myocardial infarction 1 month ago. His history is notable for urticaria and dyspnea after taking ibuprofen on two occasions. At follow-up, low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention is being considered. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoid aspirin because NSAID hypersensitivity contraindicates it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start 325 mg enteric-coated to bypass the stomach

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start 81 mg because low doses avoid hypersensitivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start aspirin only after the cardiac enzymes normalize

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start aspirin together with a daily antihistamine

explanation.summary: Hypersensitivity to NSAIDs is a contraindication to aspirin use.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has had hypersensitivity reactions (urticaria, dyspnea) to an NSAID. The brick states that hypersensitivity to NSAIDs is also a contraindication for aspirin use, so aspirin should be avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enteric coating alters absorption but does not address a hypersensitivity contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low doses do not eliminate hypersensitivity risk; the contraindication applies regardless of dose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Timing relative to cardiac enzymes is irrelevant to the contraindication posed by NSAID hypersensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antihistamine co-administration is not described as a way to safely give aspirin to a patient with NSAID hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man who began taking aspirin 3 days ago for chronic back pain presents with hematemesis. A colleague suggests that aspirin cannot be responsible because the exposure has been too brief. Which of the following statements about aspirin's gastrointestinal adverse effects is accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GI injury can occur within minutes to months of use

choices.label: B
choices.text: GI injury is eliminated by using 81 mg daily

choices.label: C
choices.text: GI injury occurs only at doses above 1300 mg daily

choices.label: D
choices.text: GI injury occurs only with enteric-coated preparations

choices.label: E
choices.text: GI injury requires at least 6 months of continuous therapy

explanation.summary: Aspirin's GI adverse effects (ulcer, erosive gastritis, upper GI bleeding) can occur within minutes to months of use.
explanation.whyCorrect: GI-related effects are the most common adverse drug reactions with aspirin, occurring mainly in the stomach as ulcer, erosive gastritis, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The brick specifies that these GI ADRs can occur within minutes to months of use, so 3 days of therapy is fully compatible with aspirin-related upper GI bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lower doses produce fewer side effects, but the brick does not state that 81 mg eliminates GI injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GI injury is not restricted to very high doses; it results from prostaglandin inhibition at ordinary doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enteric coating is not a prerequisite for GI injury, which reflects loss of protective prostaglandins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No minimum duration is required; injury can appear within minutes of use.

questions.stem: A pharmacist screens several patients who have asked about taking aspirin. Aspirin may be given to which of the following patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An 8-year-old girl with fever from influenza

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 31-year-old man with asthma, rhinitis, and nasal polyps

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 55-year-old man who smokes cigarettes daily

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 62-year-old woman with an active gastric ulcer

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 70-year-old man with severe renal failure

explanation.summary: Smoking is not a contraindication to aspirin, whereas febrile children, the asthma-rhinitis-nasal polyp triad, active peptic ulcer disease, and severe renal failure are.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review material states that smoking is not a contraindication to aspirin. Each of the other patients has a listed contraindication, so the smoker is the only one to whom aspirin may be given.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin is contraindicated in febrile children because of the risk of Reye's syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin is contraindicated in patients with asthma, rhinitis, and nasal polyps because of AERD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Active peptic ulcer disease contraindicates aspirin because of increased bleeding risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severe liver or renal failure is listed among the contraindications to aspirin.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist maps the tissue distribution of the prostanoids generated downstream of cyclooxygenase. Which of the following prostanoids is produced predominantly in mast cells, brain, and airways?

explanation.summary: PGD2 is the tissue-specific prostaglandin of mast cells, brain, and airways.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's figure, PGH2 is converted to tissue-specific prostaglandins. PGD2 is assigned to mast cells, brain, and airways, distinguishing it from the other COX products.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PGI2 is produced in endothelium, blood vessels, platelets, kidney, and brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PGE2 is produced in pain receptors, brain, kidneys, blood vessels, and platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PGF2-alpha is produced in pain receptors, uterus, airways, and eyes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is produced in platelets, blood vessels, macrophages, and kidney.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman takes aspirin for a headache. By acetylating cyclooxygenase, aspirin blocks the conversion of arachidonic acid into which of the following immediate products?

explanation.summary: COX-1 and COX-2 convert arachidonic acid to PGH2, the precursor of the tissue-specific prostaglandins and thromboxane A2.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's figure, phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid, which COX-1 and COX-2 convert to PGH2. PGH2 is then converted to tissue-specific prostaglandins (PGD2, PGE2, PGF2-alpha, PGI2) and thromboxane A2. Aspirin, by inhibiting COX, blocks the arachidonic acid to PGH2 step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukotriene B4 is a lipoxygenase product, not the product of the COX step that aspirin blocks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoxin A4 is not the immediate COX product of arachidonic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phosphatidylcholine is a membrane phospholipid upstream of arachidonic acid, not a product of COX.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet-activating factor is not generated by cyclooxygenase from arachidonic acid.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man takes low-dose aspirin daily. Within his platelets, aspirin acetylates the cyclooxygenase-1 enzyme. Which of the following best describes the fate of platelet COX-1 after this acetylation?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversible inhibition until aspirin is cleared

explanation.summary: Acetylation of COX-1 by aspirin completely inactivates the enzyme, whereas acetylation of COX-2 switches its catalytic activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that once acetylated, COX-1 is completely inactivated. This contrasts with COX-2, whose acetylation converts its activity from a cyclooxygenase to a lipoxygenase. Because platelets cannot make new enzyme, this inactivation lasts for the platelet's lifespan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Platelets are non-nucleated and lack DNA for transcription, so they cannot make new enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conversion to lipoxygenase activity is the fate of acetylated COX-2, not COX-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inactivated COX-1 cannot produce PGH2; its output falls, it does not rise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspirin's inhibition of COX-1 is irreversible, not reversible; the brick's review questions explicitly reject reversible COX-1 inhibition.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to classify aspirin according to its action on the arachidonic acid pathway. Which of the following best classifies aspirin?

explanation.summary: Aspirin is a non-selective COX inhibitor and a salicylate belonging to the NSAID class.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick classifies aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) as a member of the NSAID class, a non-selective COX inhibitor, and a salicylate. Chemically it is acetylsalicylate, and it acetylates both COX-1 and COX-2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin does not block leukotriene receptors; in AERD it actually increases pro-inflammatory leukotrienes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin does not inhibit lipoxygenase; acetylated COX-2 actually acquires lipoxygenase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase A2, which releases arachidonic acid, is not aspirin's target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspirin acetylates both COX-1 and COX-2; it is not selective for COX-2.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is recovering from varicella; his fever resolved 1 week ago and his lesions are crusting. He sprains his ankle playing soccer, and his mother asks whether she can now give him aspirin for the pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin is acceptable at a reduced 81 mg once-daily dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspirin is acceptable if an enteric-coated tablet is used instead

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aspirin is acceptable if it is taken with food and a full glass of water

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aspirin is acceptable now that the fever has resolved and lesions are crusting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aspirin remains contraindicated during recovery from a viral infection

explanation.summary: Salicylates are contraindicated in children both during and while recovering from viral infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of the possibility of Reye's syndrome, the brick states that aspirin and other salicylates are contraindicated in infants, children, and children recovering from and during viral infections (under 18 years). Resolution of the fever does not lift the contraindication in a child still recovering from varicella.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dose reduction does not eliminate the Reye's syndrome risk in a child.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enteric coating changes absorption, not the pediatric contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Taking aspirin with food addresses gastric irritation, not the risk of Reye's syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The contraindication explicitly extends to children recovering from viral infections, not just febrile ones.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with fever and sore throat from a viral upper respiratory infection asks her physician whether she can take aspirin, noting that she is nearly an adult. The physician advises against it. Salicylates are contraindicated in febrile patients with viral infections who are younger than which of the following ages?

explanation.summary: Because of Reye's syndrome, aspirin and other salicylates are contraindicated in infants, children, and adolescents under 18 years during and after viral infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifies that, due to the possibility of Reye's syndrome, aspirin and other salicylates are contraindicated in infants, children, and children recovering from and during viral infections, defining the group as those under 18 years. A 17-year-old with a febrile viral illness therefore falls within the contraindication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cutoff is not limited to infants under 2 years; it extends through adolescence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 6-year-old is included, but the contraindication continues well beyond 6 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Twelve years is not the upper limit given; the brick uses under 18 years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sixteen years understates the stated cutoff, which is under 18 years.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man ingests two aspirin tablets. After absorption, aspirin is hydrolyzed to its principal circulating salicylate. Which of the following compounds is formed by this hydrolysis?

explanation.summary: Aspirin (acetylsalicylate) is hydrolyzed to salicylic acid, which is then conjugated and cleared renally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that aspirin is hydrolyzed to salicylic acid and is cleared renally, with the hydrolysis following first-order kinetics. The salicylate then undergoes phase II reactions before renal excretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaminophen is a separate analgesic, not a metabolite of aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gentisic acid is not the product of aspirin hydrolysis described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methyl salicylate is a different salicylate ester, not a hydrolysis product of aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salicyluric acid is not the hydrolysis product the brick names; hydrolysis of acetylsalicylate yields salicylic acid.

questions.stem: An allergist reviews the epidemiology of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with a group of residents. Which of the following best describes the typical age at which this condition presents?

explanation.summary: AERD presents from late childhood to adulthood, with a median age of onset around 34 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that AERD presents during late childhood to adulthood, with the median age of onset around 34 years. Nasal congestion and rhinorrhea are usually the first symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although onset can begin in late childhood, the median age is 34, not 14.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AERD is not a disease of early childhood; the median onset is in the fourth decade.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AERD does not present in infancy; infancy is instead the period of concern for Reye's syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A median onset in the 60s is later than the brick's stated median of about 34 years.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a known inherited bleeding disorder asks whether he can take aspirin for occasional headaches. His physician tells him aspirin is contraindicated. Which of the following properties of aspirin best explains this contraindication?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It chelates calcium required for coagulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits hepatic synthesis of clotting factors

explanation.summary: Bleeding disorders contraindicate aspirin because aspirin irreversibly inhibits thromboxane A2 and thus platelet aggregation for the platelet's lifespan.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists bleeding disorders among aspirin's contraindications. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits TxA2, which is important for platelet aggregation, and because platelets cannot synthesize new COX the effect lasts about 7-10 days. Adding this antiplatelet effect to a preexisting bleeding tendency increases bleeding risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin does not activate fibrinolysis; it prevents platelet aggregation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking vitamin K epoxide reductase is the mechanism of warfarin, not aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium chelation is not a property of aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspirin does not impair hepatic clotting factor synthesis; its hemostatic effect is on platelets.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had persistent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and postnasal drip for the past year, and nasal polyps were recently identified. She has no history of asthma or drug reactions. If she is developing aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, asthma would be expected to develop, on average, how long after her initial upper respiratory tract symptoms?

explanation.summary: In AERD, asthma develops on average about 2 years after the initial upper respiratory tract symptoms, and aspirin intolerance usually about 4 years later.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation describes the AERD timeline: nasal congestion and rhinorrhea appear first, asthma can develop on average 2 years after the initial upper respiratory tract symptoms, and aspirin intolerance can also occur, usually 4 years later.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two months is not the interval described; asthma follows the nasal symptoms by about 2 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two weeks is far shorter than the average 2-year interval to asthma onset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Six months understates the average interval between sinonasal symptoms and asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ten years overstates the interval; asthma appears at about 2 years and aspirin intolerance at about 4 years.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman takes acetaminophen for a headache and low-grade fever. Unlike ibuprofen, acetaminophen produces little anti-inflammatory effect at a site of peripheral tissue inflammation. Which of the following best describes acetaminophen's mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antagonism of prostaglandin receptors on peripheral pain fibers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of phospholipase A2, preventing arachidonic acid release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible acetylation of cyclooxygenase in platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selective inhibition of COX-2 in peripheral tissues

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen is a weak, non-competitive, reversible COX inhibitor that acts mainly centrally, giving analgesic and antipyretic but weak peripheral anti-inflammatory effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acetaminophen is oxidized by the brain CYP450 system, and the oxidized form inhibits COX at its peroxidase catalytic site within the CNS. Because its peripheral COX inhibition is weak, it relieves pain and fever but has little anti-inflammatory action, and it is not classified as an NSAID.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It inhibits cyclooxygenase rather than antagonizing prostaglandin receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetaminophen inhibits COX itself, not the upstream enzyme phospholipase A2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irreversible platelet COX acetylation describes aspirin; acetaminophen is a weak, reversible inhibitor and lacks antiplatelet activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetaminophen is a non-selective COX inhibitor, not a selective COX-2 inhibitor.

questions.stem: A patient asks whether acetaminophen will 'thin the blood' the way aspirin does. Which of the following best explains why acetaminophen lacks meaningful antiplatelet, antithrombotic activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High peroxidase levels in platelets block its cyclooxygenase-inhibiting action

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a selective COX-2 inhibitor that spares platelet COX-1 entirely

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is cleared too rapidly to reach circulating platelets in the portal circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It selectively spares COX-1 in all peripheral tissues including platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets do not express cyclooxygenase and so cannot make thromboxane

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen does not act as an antithrombotic agent because platelets contain high levels of peroxidase that prevent it from inhibiting COX there.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that higher levels of peroxidase in platelets block acetaminophen from acting on platelet COX, so it does not inhibit thromboxane production and has no antithrombotic effect, unlike aspirin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: It is not a selective COX-2 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Its lack of platelet effect is due to platelet peroxidase, not rapid clearance; acetaminophen distributes widely into body fluids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetaminophen is a non-selective COX inhibitor, not a COX-1-sparing agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets do express cyclooxygenase and produce thromboxane A2; acetaminophen simply cannot inhibit it effectively there.

questions.stem: A healthy adult with no liver disease asks about the maximum amount of acetaminophen that is safe to take in a single day. Which of the following is the recommended maximum daily dose?

explanation.summary: The recommended maximum daily dose of acetaminophen in healthy adults is 4 grams.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states acetaminophen is generally well tolerated when taken at recommended doses and should not exceed 4 grams per day; exceeding this, especially with combination products, risks hepatotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1 gram is a common single dose, not the daily maximum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 2 grams is below the stated 4-gram daily limit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 8 grams exceeds the recommended maximum and risks hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 12 grams greatly exceeds the safe limit and is well into the overdose range.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. Which of the following metabolites is directly responsible for the resulting hepatotoxicity?

explanation.summary: NAPQI is the toxic metabolite formed via the CYP450 pathway that causes acetaminophen-induced liver injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: A minor CYP450 (CYP2E1) route converts acetaminophen to the potentially toxic NAPQI. In overdose, NAPQI accumulates, covalently binds hepatic proteins, and causes oxidative stress and centrilobular necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The glucuronide conjugate is a nontoxic Phase II product, not the injurious metabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sulfate conjugate is also a nontoxic Phase II product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutathione is protective; it conjugates and detoxifies NAPQI rather than causing harm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transaminases are hepatic enzymes released as markers of injury, not metabolites of acetaminophen.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents 8 hours after ingesting a large amount of acetaminophen. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which the overdose produces hepatocellular injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of nontoxic glucuronide conjugates overwhelms the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: An immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction destroys hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct inhibition of COX-2 within hepatocytes causes cell death

choices.label: D
choices.text: Massive prostaglandin release triggers hepatic inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saturation of conjugation shunts the drug to CYP450, generating NAPQI

explanation.summary: In overdose, the sulfation and glucuronidation pathways saturate, shifting metabolism toward CYP2E1 and NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and injures hepatocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: When toxic amounts are ingested, the Phase II conjugation pathways are saturated, so more drug is oxidized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI. NAPQI depletes glutathione, then covalently binds hepatic proteins, producing oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, and centrilobular necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucuronide conjugates are nontoxic; the problem is diversion to the NAPQI pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The injury is a dose-dependent toxic (metabolic) mechanism, not an immune hypersensitivity reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Injury is due to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, not direct COX-2 inhibition in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatotoxicity results from NAPQI adduct formation, not from prostaglandin-driven inflammation.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use is brought in after an acetaminophen overdose and develops severe liver injury sooner than expected. Which of the following best explains his increased susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol blocks intestinal absorption of the antidote

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol competes for glucuronidation, raising plasma drug levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alcohol displaces acetaminophen from plasma proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alcohol inhibits renal clearance of acetaminophen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1 and lowers glutathione reserves

explanation.summary: Chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1 and is associated with poor nutrition that lowers glutathione, both of which increase NAPQI-mediated hepatotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1, increasing conversion of acetaminophen to NAPQI, and is often associated with poor nutrition that reduces glutathione reserves. Together these raise the risk of hepatotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol increases hepatotoxicity through NAPQI, not by blocking N-acetylcysteine absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The described mechanism is CYP2E1 induction, not competition for glucuronidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma protein displacement is not the mechanism described for alcohol-related risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The increased risk is from enhanced NAPQI formation, not impaired renal clearance.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man being treated for latent tuberculosis uses acetaminophen for musculoskeletal pain. Which of the following medications in his regimen most increases his risk of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity?

explanation.summary: Isoniazid increases the risk of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity by increasing the amount of NAPQI produced in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists isoniazid (a tuberculosis medication) as one of the few drugs that increase acetaminophen's hepatotoxicity risk by raising hepatic NAPQI production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutathione is protective, detoxifying NAPQI rather than increasing injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote; it restores glutathione and reduces NAPQI, lowering rather than raising risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ondansetron is an antiemetic with no described effect on acetaminophen metabolism or hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetaminophen can potentiate warfarin's anticoagulant effect and raise bleeding risk, but warfarin does not increase hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman stabilized on warfarin begins taking acetaminophen regularly for chronic knee pain, and her INR rises. Which of the following best describes this interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaminophen can increase warfarin's anticoagulant effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetaminophen causes warfarin to become directly hepatotoxic

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acetaminophen induces enzymes that clear warfarin faster, lowering the INR

choices.label: E
choices.text: There is no clinically relevant interaction between the two drugs

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen can increase the effect of warfarin, potentially leading to increased anticoagulation and bleeding, so the warfarin dose may need adjustment.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states acetaminophen can increase the effects of the anticoagulant warfarin, potentially increasing anticoagulation and bleeding risk, so a patient's warfarin dose may need to be adjusted.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Warfarin does not become hepatotoxic; the concern is enhanced anticoagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione displacement is not the mechanism of the warfarin interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The interaction increases anticoagulation and INR, it does not accelerate warfarin clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick specifically notes a clinically relevant interaction requiring possible dose adjustment.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with a confirmed acetaminophen overdose is given N-acetylcysteine. Which of the following best describes how this antidote reduces hepatic injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It adsorbs acetaminophen in the gut to prevent absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly binds and inactivates circulating NAPQI in the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: It enhances renal excretion of unchanged acetaminophen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It irreversibly inhibits CYP2E1 to stop all further metabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It provides cysteine that helps restore glutathione

explanation.summary: N-acetylcysteine supplies cysteine to help restore glutathione, which decreases toxic NAPQI levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states NAC provides the cysteine that helps restore glutathione levels, resulting in a decrease in toxic NAPQI; it also scavenges free radicals and increases mitochondrial ATP production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gut adsorption describes activated charcoal, not N-acetylcysteine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NAC works by replenishing glutathione, not by directly binding NAPQI in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The described mechanism is glutathione restoration, not enhanced renal excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its benefit comes from restoring glutathione, not from irreversibly inhibiting CYP2E1.

questions.stem: A patient presents after an acetaminophen overdose, and the diagnosis is confirmed by history and serum drug levels. To best prevent severe hepatotoxicity, N-acetylcysteine should be administered within which of the following windows after the overdose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At any time within the first 5 days, timing does not matter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only if the patient becomes symptomatic

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only once acute liver failure has developed

explanation.summary: N-acetylcysteine should be given promptly, preferably within the first 16 hours after the overdose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that once overdose is established, NAC should promptly be given, preferably within the first 16 hours after the overdose, to restore glutathione and reduce NAPQI before severe injury occurs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Timing does matter; early administration within about 16 hours is emphasized.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Waiting 48 hours delays treatment past the preferred early window and worsens outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treatment should not be delayed until symptoms appear given the preferred early window.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAC is meant to prevent hepatotoxicity, so it should not be withheld until liver failure develops.

questions.stem: A toxicologist plots a patient's serum acetaminophen concentration against the time since ingestion to decide whether antidotal therapy is needed. Which of the following best describes the purpose of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It determines the correct therapeutic dose of acetaminophen to prescribe

choices.label: B
choices.text: It estimates renal function to guide drug clearance

choices.label: C
choices.text: It measures the patient's hepatic glutathione stores directly

choices.label: D
choices.text: It predicts the gastrointestinal toxicity of NSAIDs

choices.label: E
choices.text: It predicts the risk of hepatotoxicity

explanation.summary: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram relates serum acetaminophen concentration to time since ingestion to predict the risk of hepatotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the nomogram as relating serum acetaminophen concentration to the time of ingestion as a predictor of hepatotoxicity; patients below the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line generally do not develop severe hepatotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is a risk-prediction tool for overdose, not a dosing chart for therapeutic use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It addresses hepatotoxicity risk, not renal function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It uses serum drug concentration and timing, not a direct measure of glutathione stores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It applies to acetaminophen overdose, not NSAID gastrointestinal toxicity.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department several hours after ingesting a large quantity of acetaminophen tablets. She reports abdominal pain and intractable nausea and vomiting, and examination reveals a tender hepatic edge. Which of the following laboratory findings is most consistent with her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A falling hematocrit from gastrointestinal hemorrhage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Markedly elevated serum amylase from acute pancreatitis

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen overdose presents with abdominal pain, intractable nausea and vomiting, and a tender hepatic edge, with serum transaminases that can rise rapidly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes overdose patients presenting with abdominal pain, intractable nausea and vomiting, and a tender hepatic edge on exam, noting that serum transaminases can rise rapidly and severe cases progress to acute liver failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The injury is hepatocellular rather than from gastrointestinal bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiac injury with troponin elevation is not a feature of acetaminophen overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetaminophen toxicity targets the liver, not the pancreas, so a rise in amylase is not expected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia is not the described pattern of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to explain why acetaminophen and the NSAIDs both reduce prostaglandin synthesis yet differ in where they act on the cyclooxygenase enzyme. Acetaminophen inhibits COX activity in the central nervous system at which of the following locations on the enzyme?

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen inhibits COX at the peroxidase catalytic site rather than the cyclooxygenase catalytic site targeted by NSAIDs.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the CNS, acetaminophen is oxidized by the brain CYP450 system and the oxidized form inhibits COX activity. The brick specifies that enzyme function is inhibited at the peroxidase catalytic site rather than the COX catalytic site, which is one reason acetaminophen binds at a different COX site than NSAIDs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not describe acetaminophen blocking the arachidonic acid channel; it names the peroxidase site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cyclooxygenase catalytic site is where NSAIDs act; acetaminophen's binding there in peripheral tissues is weak.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An allosteric site is not the mechanism described; inhibition occurs at the peroxidase catalytic site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The membrane-anchoring domain is not the site of acetaminophen's action.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman takes acetaminophen for a tension headache. The drug's analgesic effect depends on a chemical change it undergoes within the central nervous system before it can inhibit cyclooxygenase. Which of the following best describes this step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetylation by platelet peroxidase into a reactive imine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion to a glucuronide conjugate that binds COX

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidation by the brain cytochrome P450 system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduction by glutathione to an active thiol metabolite

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfation by hepatic transferases before crossing into the CNS

explanation.summary: In the CNS, acetaminophen is oxidized by the brain CYP450 system, and the oxidized form is what inhibits COX.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acetaminophen's effects are primarily central: in the CNS the drug is oxidized by the brain CYP450 system and the oxidized form of the drug inhibits COX activity at the peroxidase catalytic site. This central activation explains its analgesic and antipyretic effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Platelet peroxidase blocks acetaminophen from acting; it does not activate the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucuronide conjugates are nontoxic products destined for excretion and do not inhibit COX.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutathione conjugates NAPQI for detoxification; it does not generate the active central form of the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfation is a hepatic Phase II conjugation that produces safe metabolites for excretion, not an activating step in the CNS.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a warm, swollen knee from an acute inflammatory flare has been taking acetaminophen at recommended doses. Her pain improves modestly but the swelling and warmth persist, whereas a course of naproxen previously reduced both. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaminophen cannot cross into inflamed synovial fluid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetaminophen has only limited inhibition of peripheral COX

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acetaminophen is inactivated by leukocyte myeloperoxidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acetaminophen selectively spares COX-2 in peripheral tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acetaminophen stimulates phospholipase A2 in inflamed joints

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen's limited peripheral COX inhibition explains its analgesic and antipyretic effects but weak anti-inflammatory effects compared with NSAIDs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acetaminophen's effects are primarily central, with weak peripheral effects on COX function. Its limited peripheral COX inhibition helps explain why it relieves pain and fever but has weak anti-inflammatory activity, so tissue inflammation is not controlled the way an NSAID like naproxen controls it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaminophen distributes widely into body fluids; poor penetration is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukocyte myeloperoxidase inactivation is not described; the brick attributes the weak effect to limited peripheral COX inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetaminophen is a non-selective COX inhibitor; it does not spare COX-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetaminophen does not stimulate phospholipase A2 or arachidonic acid release.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with no liver disease takes acetaminophen 1 g every 8 hours for 3 days after a dental procedure. Which of the following adverse effects is he most likely to experience at this dosing?

explanation.summary: At recommended doses acetaminophen is well tolerated; its usual adverse effects are mild nausea, GI upset, rash or other hypersensitivity, itching, and headache.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states acetaminophen causes fewer adverse effects than NSAIDs, usually mild nausea, GI upset, rash and other hypersensitivity reactions, itching, and headache. At 3 g/day, below the 4 g/day limit, mild nausea is the most likely of the listed effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abnormal bruising is a rare, serious adverse effect rather than a common one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute liver failure follows overdose, not 3 g/day in a patient without liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute renal failure is rare and serious, not expected at recommended doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Jaundice is listed among the rare but serious adverse effects, not the common ones.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presents 3 days after an unrecognized acetaminophen overdose and now has jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy consistent with acute liver failure. His family asks about prognosis. Once acute liver failure has developed after acetaminophen overdose, the mortality rate rises to approximately which of the following?

explanation.summary: Mortality from acetaminophen overdose is low with early detection, but once acute liver failure occurs the mortality rate increases to 28%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mortality rates are lower with early detection; however, if acute liver failure occurs, the mortality rate increases to 28%. This is why prompt recognition and early NAC administration matter.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2% understates the mortality of established acute liver failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5% is the mortality cited for untreated patients above the probable hepatic toxicity nomogram line, not for established acute liver failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 10% is not the figure given; it is roughly the share of acetaminophen normally metabolized via the CYP450 pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 18% is not the mortality figure cited for acute liver failure.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old college student with a cold is taking acetaminophen 500 mg tablets and has also purchased an over-the-counter liquid cold product containing acetaminophen, doxylamine, and dextromethorphan. Which of the following is the most important counseling point to prevent harm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Account for the acetaminophen in every product so the daily total stays under 4 g

choices.label: B
choices.text: Separate the tablets and the liquid by at least 4 hours to avoid absorption competition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stop the tablets because dextromethorphan blocks acetaminophen metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take both products with food to prevent gastric ulceration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the liquid product only at bedtime to avoid sedation

explanation.summary: Unintentional overdose is common because acetaminophen is widely available OTC in many single-ingredient and combination products, so the total from all products must stay under the daily limit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that unintentional overdoses occur because acetaminophen is in many single-ingredient and combination products, including cold and flu preparations and opioid combinations, and that maximum daily (4 g/day) limits are provided on the label for this reason. The key intervention is recognizing the hidden acetaminophen in the combination product and keeping the total under 4 g/day.

whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no described absorption competition; the concern is cumulative dose, not timing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dextromethorphan is not described as affecting acetaminophen metabolism; the drugs that raise risk are isoniazid, carbamazepine, and alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric ulceration is an NSAID concern; acetaminophen's key risk here is hepatotoxicity from excess total dose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Timing the dose for sedation does not address the risk of exceeding the acetaminophen daily limit.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman takes a 1 g oral dose of acetaminophen for fever. Peak plasma concentrations of the drug are expected within approximately which of the following time intervals?

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen has good bioavailability with peak concentrations within 30-60 minutes, a half-life of about 2 hours, and wide distribution into body fluids.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acetaminophen has good bioavailability and that peak concentrations can be reached within 30-60 minutes. It adds that the half-life is approximately 2 hours and that the drug distributes widely into body fluids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2-4 hours is later than the stated peak; 2 hours is approximately the half-life.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5-10 minutes is too fast for an oral dose; the stated peak is 30-60 minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 6-8 hours is far beyond the stated time to peak concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 10-20 minutes is earlier than the stated time to peak.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommate, who found an empty bottle of acetaminophen. The patient is drowsy and gives an inconsistent account of what he took. Which of the following is required to establish the diagnosis of acetaminophen overdose and guide antidote therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: History combined with serum acetaminophen levels

explanation.summary: The diagnosis of acetaminophen overdose is established by history and serum drug levels, after which NAC should promptly be given.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that once the diagnosis of acetaminophen overdose is established (history, serum drug levels), the antidote NAC should promptly be given, preferably within 16 hours. Serum concentration plotted against time since ingestion on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram predicts hepatotoxicity risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Liver biopsy is not part of the diagnostic approach described; centrilobular necrosis is the late pathologic result, not the diagnostic test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP2E1 activity is a risk modifier, not a diagnostic measurement used in overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AST greater than 1000 IU/L defines severe hepatotoxicity in nomogram data; it is a consequence, and waiting for it would delay the antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine glutathione conjugate measurement is not described as a diagnostic tool.

questions.stem: A healthy adult takes a therapeutic dose of acetaminophen. Which of the following pathways accounts for the largest fraction of the drug's metabolism?

explanation.summary: Most acetaminophen undergoes Phase II conjugation, roughly 45-55% via glucuronidation and 30-40% via sulfation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that most acetaminophen undergoes Phase II conjugation, approximately 45-55% via glucuronidation and 30-40% via sulfation, producing safe metabolites for excretion. Glucuronidation is therefore the largest single route at therapeutic doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutathione conjugation handles only the small NAPQI fraction produced by CYP450.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The CYP450 (CYP2E1) route is only about 5-10% of metabolism normally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick describes metabolism as occurring mainly in the liver by conjugation, not excretion of unchanged drug as the dominant route.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfation accounts for about 30-40%, a smaller share than glucuronidation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man takes acetaminophen at recommended doses. The small fraction of drug converted to NAPQI by the cytochrome P450 pathway does not cause liver injury. Which of the following best explains why NAPQI is harmless under these conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NAPQI covalently binds plasma albumin and is excreted

choices.label: B
choices.text: NAPQI is conjugated with glutathione to form safe metabolites for excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: NAPQI is produced only in the CNS, where hepatocytes are not exposed

choices.label: D
choices.text: NAPQI is rapidly glucuronidated before it can bind proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: NAPQI is re-reduced to acetaminophen by hepatic sulfotransferases

explanation.summary: At therapeutic doses, the roughly 10% of acetaminophen converted to NAPQI is normally conjugated with glutathione, producing safe metabolites for excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the CYP450 route as usually only about 10% of acetaminophen excretion and states that the potentially toxic NAPQI is normally conjugated with glutathione, yielding safe metabolites for excretion. Toxicity arises only when NAPQI production outstrips glutathione supply.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Covalent binding of NAPQI to hepatic proteins is the mechanism of injury, not of safe elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAPQI is generated in the liver by the hepatic CYP450 system, where hepatocytes are directly exposed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucuronidation acts on the parent drug, not on NAPQI; glutathione handles NAPQI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfotransferases conjugate the parent drug; they do not reduce NAPQI back to acetaminophen.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a long history of severe malnutrition and very low body weight is admitted after an acetaminophen overdose and develops hepatotoxicity at a lower ingested dose than expected. Which of the following best explains her heightened susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated hepatic peroxidase converts NAPQI into an even more reactive form

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired sulfation causes accumulation of the parent drug in adipose tissue stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased renal tubular reabsorption of filtered acetaminophen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of platelet peroxidase permits widespread systemic COX inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced glucuronidation shifts metabolism toward microsomal NAPQI production

explanation.summary: In a malnourished state, glucuronidation of acetaminophen is reduced, leading to enhanced microsomal metabolism and increased NAPQI production, while glutathione reserves are also lower.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in a malnourished state glucuronidation of acetaminophen is reduced, which leads to enhanced microsomal metabolism and increased production of NAPQI, predisposing these patients to liver toxicity. Poor nutrition also reduces glutathione reserves needed to detoxify NAPQI.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NAPQI itself is the reactive metabolite; no further peroxidase activation is described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes reduced glucuronidation shunting drug to the CYP pathway, not adipose accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal reabsorption is not the described mechanism; the issue is a metabolic shift toward NAPQI.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet peroxidase relates to acetaminophen's lack of antithrombotic effect, not to hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: Two patients present with acetaminophen overdoses of similar magnitude and timing: a 22-year-old woman and a 55-year-old man, neither with alcohol use or liver disease. Based on age alone, the older patient is at greater risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute liver failure, liver transplantation, and death

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced glucuronidation that masks early transaminase rise

choices.label: C
choices.text: Falsely low readings on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slower absorption and a delayed peak concentration

explanation.summary: Adults over 40 years of age have a greater risk of acute liver failure, liver transplantation, and death following acetaminophen overdose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the factors that impact acetaminophen toxicity, the brick notes that adults over 40 years of age have a greater risk of acute liver failure, liver transplantation, and death following overdose, independent of the alcohol and nutrition factors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Age is associated with worse outcomes, not with enhanced glucuronidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nomogram relates serum concentration to time since ingestion and is not described as being altered by age.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAC adverse reactions (flushing, urticaria, rash) are not described as age-dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick does not describe age-related changes in absorption or time to peak.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with epilepsy well controlled on an antiepileptic drug develops hepatotoxicity after taking acetaminophen in amounts only modestly above the recommended limit. Which of the following medications in his regimen most likely increased his risk?

explanation.summary: Carbamazepine, an antiepileptic, increases acetaminophen's risk of hepatotoxicity by increasing the amount of NAPQI produced in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists isoniazid, carbamazepine (an antiepileptic), and alcohol as agents that increase acetaminophen's risk of hepatotoxicity by increasing hepatic NAPQI production. In a patient on antiepileptic therapy, carbamazepine is the relevant interacting drug.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dextromethorphan is a cough suppressant in combination products and is not described as increasing hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxylamine appears in OTC combination products but is not described as raising NAPQI production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote and lowers NAPQI; it is not a risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin's interaction is increased anticoagulation and bleeding, not hepatotoxicity, and it is not an antiepileptic.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman ingests a large quantity of acetaminophen. Within which of the following windows after ingestion would abdominal pain, intractable nausea and vomiting, and a tender hepatic edge typically appear?

explanation.summary: The clinical picture of acetaminophen overdose, with abdominal pain, intractable nausea and vomiting, and a tender hepatic edge, appears within the first 24-72 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in an acetaminophen overdose patients present with abdominal pain, intractable nausea and vomiting, and a tender hepatic edge on physical exam within the first 24-72 hours, with transaminases rising rapidly and severe cases progressing to acute liver failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two weeks is far beyond the described time course.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Days 5-7 is later than the described onset of the presenting symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1-2 hours corresponds to the drug reaching peak concentration, not to the hepatic symptoms described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 6-12 hours is earlier than the 24-72 hour window the brick gives for these findings.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man receiving N-acetylcysteine for an acetaminophen overdose develops facial flushing and hives. Which of the following best characterizes these reactions to NAC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are caused by glutathione depletion from excess cysteine

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are uncommon adverse reactions, each occurring in 8% or fewer patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: They indicate NAC-induced hepatotoxicity and require stopping the antidote

choices.label: D
choices.text: They occur in roughly half of treated patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: They signal that the acetaminophen level has risen above the treatment line

explanation.summary: NAC adverse reactions are not common; facial flushing (8% or less), urticaria (8% or less), and rash (4%) are the ones described.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that although not common, NAC can cause adverse reactions, with the common ones being facial flushing (less than or equal to 8%), urticaria (less than or equal to 8%), and rash (4%). Flushing and hives in this patient fit that profile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NAC supplies cysteine to restore glutathione; it does not deplete it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAC protects the liver by restoring glutathione; flushing and urticaria are not signs of hepatotoxicity from the antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stated frequencies are 8% or less, far from half of patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These reactions are drug adverse effects unrelated to the patient's nomogram position.

questions.stem: Beyond replenishing glutathione, N-acetylcysteine has additional effects that support hepatocytes during acetaminophen toxicity. Which of the following is one of these additional actions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chelation of NAPQI-protein adducts for biliary excretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition of acetaminophen absorption from the gut

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of glucuronidation to divert drug away from CYP2E1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scavenging of free radicals and increased mitochondrial ATP production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of hepatocyte COX-2 to promote regeneration

explanation.summary: In addition to restoring glutathione, NAC has been shown to scavenge free radicals and increase mitochondrial ATP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that NAC provides cysteine to restore glutathione and decrease NAPQI, and that it has also been shown to scavenge free radicals and increase mitochondrial ATP production. These actions counter the oxidative stress and mitochondrial damage caused by NAPQI adducts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chelation of adducts is not a described action; NAC prevents adduct formation by restoring glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NAC does not block gut absorption of acetaminophen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAC does not act by inducing glucuronidation; it works downstream on NAPQI and oxidative injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NAC has no described effect on hepatocyte COX-2.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents 4 hours after an acetaminophen ingestion. Her serum acetaminophen concentration is 340 mcg/mL, placing her above the line joining 300 mcg/mL at 4 hours and 37.5 mcg/mL at 16 hours on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Which of the following best describes her risk and management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 28% mortality; liver transplantation evaluation should precede any NAC administration

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5% mortality; repeat the serum level at 16 hours before starting any antidote treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 60% risk of severe hepatotoxicity; standard weight-based NAC dosing alone is sufficient here

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 90% risk of severe hepatotoxicity; may require increased NAC dose and poison control consultation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low risk of severe hepatotoxicity; observation alone without any antidote therapy is reasonable in this case

explanation.summary: Concentrations above the high-risk line (300 mcg/mL at 4 h to 37.5 mcg/mL at 16 h) carry a 90% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and up to 24% mortality if untreated, and may require increased acetylcysteine dosing with poison control consultation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that untreated patients with concentrations above the line joining 300 mcg/mL (1980 micromol/L) at 4 hours and 37.5 mcg/mL (250 micromol/L) at 16 hours ('high hepatic toxicity' or 'high-risk ingestion') have a 90% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and a mortality rate of up to 24%. High-risk patients may require an increased dose of acetylcysteine and consultation with a regional poison control center or clinical pharmacist.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 28% is the mortality once acute liver failure has developed; NAC should be given promptly, not deferred for transplant evaluation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5% mortality is the figure for the probable-toxicity line, and NAC should be given promptly rather than delayed for a repeat level.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 60% incidence applies to patients above the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line, not the higher high-risk line; standard dosing may be insufficient here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This level is well above both nomogram lines; observation without antidote is not appropriate.

questions.stem: A toxicology fellow reviews the original data behind the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Without antidotal therapy, patients whose serum acetaminophen concentrations fell above the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line had which of the following outcomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 10% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and 1% mortality

choices.label: B
choices.text: 28% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and 10% mortality

choices.label: C
choices.text: 60% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and 5% mortality

choices.label: D
choices.text: 90% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and 24% mortality

choices.label: E
choices.text: No severe hepatotoxicity and no deaths

explanation.summary: Untreated patients above the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line had a 60% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity (AST greater than 1000 IU/L) and a 5% mortality rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that without antidotal therapy, patients with serum acetaminophen concentrations above the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line had a 60% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity, defined as AST greater than 1000 IU/L, and a mortality rate of 5%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These numbers understate the risk above the probable toxicity line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 28% is the mortality once acute liver failure develops, not an incidence figure for this nomogram line.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 90% incidence and up to 24% mortality describe the higher 'high-risk ingestion' line, not the probable toxicity line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absence of severe hepatotoxicity describes patients below the line, not above it.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man presents 6 hours after a single acute acetaminophen ingestion. His serum acetaminophen concentration plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram falls clearly below the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line. Which of the following best describes his expected outcome?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 60% chance of AST rising above 1000 IU/L

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe hepatotoxicity is not expected to develop

explanation.summary: Patients with serum acetaminophen concentrations below the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line did not develop severe hepatotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in the original nomogram data, patients with serum acetaminophen concentrations below the 'probable hepatic toxicity' line did not develop severe hepatotoxicity. The nomogram thus identifies who is at low risk as well as who needs antidotal therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 5% mortality figure applies to patients above the line, not below it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 60% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity applies to untreated patients above the probable toxicity line.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 90% incidence applies to the high-risk line, far above this patient's level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute liver failure is the outcome of severe untreated toxicity, which is not expected below the line.

questions.stem: A physician is choosing an analgesic for mild pain in several patients. In which of the following patients is acetaminophen contraindicated according to the concerns raised in this topic?

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen is contraindicated in severe hepatic dysfunction such as cirrhosis or acute hepatitis, because the drug is metabolized by the liver and hepatotoxicity is its major concern.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because acetaminophen is metabolized by the liver, caution should be used in patients with chronic alcohol use or hepatitis, and its review material specifies that acetaminophen is contraindicated in severe hepatic dysfunction, as in acute hepatitis and cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is therefore the clearest contraindication among these patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asthma is not described as a concern for acetaminophen use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute interstitial nephritis is identified as the least direct risk factor for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, not a contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diabetes is not described as a risk factor for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypertension is not described as a concern for acetaminophen use.

questions.stem: In the inflammatory pathway, diverse physical, chemical, inflammatory, and mitogenic stimuli trigger the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. Which of the following enzymes carries out this step?

explanation.summary: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; COX-1 and COX-2 then act on arachidonic acid downstream.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inflammatory pathway figure shows membrane phospholipids converted to arachidonic acid by phospholipase A2 in response to diverse physical, chemical, inflammatory, and mitogenic stimuli. Arachidonic acid is then converted by COX-1 and COX-2 to PGH2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COX-1 acts on arachidonic acid after its release, converting it to PGH2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: COX-2 likewise acts downstream on arachidonic acid, not on membrane phospholipids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostacyclin synthase produces PGI2 from PGH2, a later step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane synthase produces thromboxane A2 from PGH2, a later step.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man takes an NSAID that inhibits COX-1 and COX-2. As a direct result, the production of which of the following intermediates, the common precursor of all tissue-specific prostaglandins, is decreased?

explanation.summary: COX-1 and COX-2 convert arachidonic acid to PGH2, the common intermediate from which tissue-specific prostaglandins are made.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pathway figure shows NSAIDs inhibiting COX-1 and COX-2, which convert arachidonic acid to PGH2. PGH2 then gives rise to the tissue-specific prostaglandins PGD2, PGE2, PGF2alpha, PGI2, and thromboxane A2, so blocking COX reduces PGH2 and all its downstream products.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arachidonic acid is the substrate of COX, released upstream by phospholipase A2; COX inhibition does not reduce its formation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Membrane phospholipids are the starting material, upstream of both phospholipase A2 and COX.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PGE2 is one tissue-specific product derived from PGH2, not the common precursor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is a downstream tissue-specific product formed in platelets, not the shared intermediate.

questions.stem: A researcher studies prostanoids generated from the common intermediate PGH2 in different tissues. Which of the following products is generated in the uterus, airways, and eyes as well as at pain receptors?

explanation.summary: PGF2alpha is the tissue-specific prostaglandin associated with pain receptors, uterus, airways, and eyes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inflammatory pathway figure lists the tissue sites for each product of PGH2: PGF2alpha is generated at pain receptors, uterus, airways, and eyes, distinguishing it from the other prostanoids by its uterine and ocular sites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PGD2 is associated with mast cells, brain, and airways, not the uterus or eyes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PGE2 is associated with pain receptors, brain, kidneys, blood vessels, and platelets, not the uterus or eyes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PGI2 is associated with endothelium, blood vessels, platelets, kidney, and brain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is associated with platelets, blood vessels, macrophages, and kidney.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman dies of acute liver failure 5 days after a massive acetaminophen overdose that was not treated in time. At autopsy, which of the following hepatic findings is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffuse periportal fibrosis with regenerative nodules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Macrovesicular steatosis sparing the central zones

explanation.summary: NAPQI adducts cause oxidative stress and mitochondrial damage that produce oxidative hepatic injury and hepatocellular centrilobular necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes toxic NAPQI covalently bonding with hepatic proteins to form adducts, resulting in oxidative stress and mitochondrial damage to hepatocytes; these products lead to oxidative hepatic injury and hepatocellular centrilobular necrosis, the hallmark of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrosis with regenerative nodules describes cirrhosis, a chronic process, not acute NAPQI injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophil-rich inflammation suggests an immune hypersensitivity injury; acetaminophen injury is a dose-dependent toxic necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous bile duct inflammation is not a feature of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steatosis is not the described lesion; acetaminophen causes necrosis centered on the centrilobular zone.
